newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK market seeks deals from China growth areas.
newsitem.headline: HK market seeks deals from China growth areas.

text.p: Strong economic growth in some of China's major regions is encouraging investors to seek exposure to those areas through the initial public offering market (IPO) in Hong Kong, analysts said.

Provincial and municipal governments on the mainland have set a clear trend in the territory of listing their business arms in order to raise capital to develop local infrastructure, local industry and the property market in their areas.
"I think it is positive for the markets," said William Lo, head of China research at Kleinwort Benson Securities.
"If they are directly investing in high growth areas (in China), it is a bit like investing in an emerging market. The growth potential is generally high in emerging markets."
New issues with exposure to high growth areas along China's coastal provinces such as Guangdong and Fujian, or major cities such as Beijing and Shanghai, are particularly attractive.

Shanghai Industrial Holdings Ltd, the investment arm of the Shanghai municipal government, is one of the most successful Hong Kong IPOs this year. The company listed in May at HK$7.28 per share and is now trading at around HK$21.00.
The company on Sunday said it would spend HK$2.7 billion to buy automotive, infrastructure, food and commercial businesses, to be paid for by issuing 162 million shares at HK$19.50 each.
Guangdong is also favoured. In a recent report, Merrill Lynch said the province had average gross domestic product per capita growth of 15.3 percent per year from 1985 to 1994.

The report said red chip conglomerate Guangdong Investment Ltd provided good exposure to the province's growth prospects with a diversified spread of businesses. More than 50 percent of the total assets of Guangdong Investment were in China, mostly in Guangdong province, as of the end of 1995.

Guangdong Investment plans to spin off its leather business arm, Guangdong Tannery Ltd, in mid-December. "The leather business has room for expansion in China and the response will depend on the pricing and the overall quality of its assets," said Chen Man Lung, analyst at China Everbright Research.

Analysts said they expected more of these companies to list in Hong Kong. "It is obvious that more Chinese companies will raise funds in Hong Kong, especially when Hong Kong becomes part of China after the handover in 1997," said Kinson Au, senior analyst at PW Asia Brokerage.
Analysts said the delay in Beijing Datang Power Generation Co's Hong Kong listing, due to poor market sentiment in the H-share market, was not indicative of an overall trend.
Beijing Datang Power said last week it was delaying its dual listing in Hong Kong and London. "I don't expect there will be much impact on the overall trend," said Chen.

But with a larger selection, investors are likely to be more choosy, focusing on promising industries. "More supply may mean more choice for investors but investors are likely to continue focusing on a fewer number of quality stocks," said Chen.

"Markets will take into consideration the earnings potential and strength of the parent. It also depends very much on their location, whether they are in a high growth area or in a remote district, as well as demand for their products."

Among upcoming listings is Hong Kong-incorporated China property development group Nam Fong International Holdings Ltd, which is expected to issue 340 million shares. Its properties mainly consist of residential developments and shopping arcades in Guangzhou city in Guangdong province.
Nam Fong's flotation is expected to run from November 26 to 29 and dealing is expected to begin on December 9.
Guangzhou Investment Co Ltd plans to spin off its China infrastructure development projects by the end of 1996 or early 1997.
